source.title: Training trajectories, mini-batch losses and the curious role of the learning rate
source.authors: Mark B. Sandler; A. Zhmoginov; Max Vladymyrov; N. Miller

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper and supplementary materials; no material truncation is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own SGD experiments on fixed mini-batches and training/validation splits, including CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and explicitly reports training losses. These conceptual results bear on V1's training-error claim, although the study focuses on averaging and learning-rate behavior rather than reproducing the version's full classification-error setup.
record.gate_note: Rows capture reported training-split loss/accuracy comparisons for averaging and learning-rate schedules, and the single-step fixed-batch loss result. Cited prior studies and unreported figure values are not treated as results. Figure 10 reports CIFAR validation accuracy only; the text says corresponding training-split results exist in supplementary materials but does not give their numerical values.
record.test_reason: The study tests mini-batch loss geometry and equivalence between weight averaging and learning-rate schedules. It does not establish CIFAR training classification error near zero, compare width, depth, initialization or normalization, or measure recovery relative to a curvature-based stability threshold. Its own results therefore test none of V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that iterate averaging has approximately equivalent learning-rate schedules in their theoretical models and ResNet experiments. They also emphasize the sharply different single-step loss behavior on the optimized mini-batch versus other training mini-batches; the latter are not validation batches.
record.recipe_differences: Uses ResNet34 with SGD momentum 0.9 on ImageNet and CIFAR datasets, often from partially trained checkpoints; investigates fixed-batch losses, averaging and learning-rate schedules rather than training from random initialization to measure classification error. Original-source claims are cited as background, not reproduced.
record.method_sensitivity: Single-step fixed-batch loss differs sharply from held-out-batch loss; the authors report that the training-versus-held-out loss-drop difference decreases for batch sizes such as 32768. Aggregation and equivalent learning-rate comparisons vary by dataset and schedule.

fits_no_version.finding: A single gradient step on a fixed ImageNet mini-batch reduces its loss from 1.8 to 0.5, while improvement on other training batches requires much smaller step sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss along a mini-batch gradient direction can fall much more on the optimized batch than on other training batches.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight averaging and corresponding reduced learning-rate side-trips produce closely matching accuracy and loss behavior on ResNet-34, including ImageNet and CIFAR validation comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Iterate averaging can approximately match the performance of specific learning-rate schedules in stochastic training.

record.problems: The main experiments start from partially trained architectures; the relevant CIFAR figure reports validation accuracy rather than training classification error. Training-split comparisons are mentioned, but the supplied text gives no numeric values for them. Several relevant accuracy/loss curves are figure-only.
record.rows_left_out: No additional numerical result rows retained. Figure 5 and Supplementary Figure 10 report validation accuracy only, while Supplementary Figure 14 plots training/validation accuracy and loss without textual numeric values; figure-only results are included where they directly expose the training split, and validation-only results are kept as context for V1.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/100 from random initialization, including random or corrupted labels, and its dependence on model size, stopping and regularization. The statement that training-split comparisons are similar concerns averaging equivalence, not near-zero error.
Teacher-student ReLU local-minimum frequencies and the effect of adding student neurons.
Training-error degradation with depth and comparisons involving identity shortcuts, special tanh initialization or Fixup.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, and initialization-dependent training speed or trainable depth.
Loss recovery or divergence relative to the initial linearized stability limit, curvature reduction, and full-batch sharpness tracking the stability threshold.
Training speed and learning-rate tolerance with versus without batch normalization, including Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for any listed version. None of its related results warrants a support, scope-limit or challenge verdict on those versions. Figure-only values unavailable in the supplied text are not evidence of absent effects.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test CIFAR-100 training classification error numerically, corrupted or random labels, model-size thresholds, SGD versus Adam, smaller-model failures, early stopping or regularized recipes. Its CIFAR-10/100 figures show validation accuracy; training-split comparisons are described but numeric values are not given.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.operation_detail: One gradient-descent step on the fixed training mini-batch using varying learning rates; measure loss on that batch.
rows.measure: Training mini-batch loss after one step
rows.value: final loss of 0.5; below the average loss of a fully trained model in a single step
rows.note: Authors state typical fully trained ImageNet loss is close to 1. This is loss, not classification error.
rows.check: The reported loss decrease from 1.8 to 0.5 is on one selected ImageNet mini-batch after a step from a partially trained checkpoint. It measures neither CIFAR training classification error nor convergence from random initialization. The value is an achievable single-step result across varied step sizes, not the endpoint of ordinary training.
